overview: Both describe how an ecosystem develops over time, but they start from very different starting points — bare rock versus already-disturbed soil.
genZNote: Primary succession starts from absolute zero, bare rock. Secondary succession gets a head start, soil's already there.

aspects.label: Starting Point
aspects.valueA: Begins on a lifeless substrate with no soil, such as bare rock or a new volcanic island.
aspects.valueB: Begins on a previously vegetated area that was disturbed, leaving soil intact (e.g. after a fire or flood).

aspects.label: Speed of the Process
aspects.valueA: Very slow, since soil must form first before larger plants can establish.
aspects.valueB: Much faster, since soil and often a seed bank already exist.

aspects.label: Example
aspects.valueA: Colonisation of bare rock after a volcanic eruption or glacial retreat.
aspects.valueB: Regrowth of a forest after a wildfire or abandoned farmland.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: Lichens are the classic pioneer species in primary succession, since they can grow directly on bare rock and begin soil formation.
overlay.memoryTrick: Primary = starting from scratch, no soil. Secondary = starting over, soil already present.
overlay.commonMisconception: Secondary succession is not automatically 'faster forever' — it's faster mainly in the early stages, thanks to pre-existing soil and surviving organisms.
